To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
weekly attenders were significantly more likely to report fish intake at least weekly and were significantly less likely report stroke, even in adjusted models, in African American women only.

weekly attendance at religious services was significantly associated with a lower prevalence of stroke in African American women and a higher prevalence of fish intake among African American women and older Mexican American men.

weekly attenders of religious services are less likely to report a history of stroke than less frequent attenders, especially in African American women, and are more likely to consume fish at least once weekly than less frequent attendees, again especially in African American and Mexican American women.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the association between religiousness and the risk of cardiovascular disease (CVD) and related factors in the US population.

the relationship between attendance of religious services and cardiovascular disease (CVD) and dietary intake and metabolic risk factors, and we have found no significant association of these variables with frequency of attendance at services.
the role of religiousness and spirituality on health.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the data do not support the hypothesis that attendance at religious services in the USA has a protective effect on cardiovascular disease, serum lipids or dietary intake.
the association of attendance frequency with cardiovascular morbidity or dietary and metabolic risk factor levels is weak or non-existent.
the association of attendance of religious service with health outcomes and dietary intake is complex, and that further research is needed.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the data do not support a strong association between frequency of attendance at church services and cardiovascular morbidity, serum lipids or dietary intake.
the frequency of attendance at church services is not a major risk factor for CHD and stroke, but may be a risk factor for diabetes in African American men and for stroke in African American women.

there is little evidence that frequency of attendance of weekly services at religious services is associated with prevalence or levels of CVD, dietary intake, or serum lipid levels in the general population.
The main takeaway from our work is that

the frequency of attendance of weekly religious services is not associated with cardiovascular disease, serum lipids, or dietary intake in representative samples of American adults, but there may be an association of weekly attendance with stroke and weekly fish intake in African American women.
the frequency of attendance at church is associated with a lower risk of stroke, particularly in African American women.

there is a need for further study of the relationship between religious attendance and health in representative samples of the population, and in particular in the African American and Hispanic subgroups.
